extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of aesthetics, psychology, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and comparing historical/philosophical theories that explain causes and conditions of laughter (derision/superiority, disappointment/incongruity, play, etc.), with empirical notes. Useful for overviewing what counts as 'comic' in theory and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derision (superiority) theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Derision or mockery is a kind of joy mixed with hate which comes from perceiving some little misfortune in a person whom we think worthy of it; laughter as 'secret elation and pride of heart' and the feeling of superiority to the object of laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulations from Hobbes/Descartes and later commentators: laughter arises from scornful pride or a feeling of surpassing/discomfiting a rival. The text notes many later writers softened or modified this harsh version and that empirical evidence (e.g., Lillien J. Martin) shows superiority is not always reported by subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeising's three-phase comic process
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is a process of three phases: (1) a shock caused by an object which seems to amount to something and yet does not; (2) a counter-shock freeing us from the deception and recognizing the nothingness of the object; (3) a happy sense of superiority to that nothingness, which makes us burst out laughing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes temporal process: surprise → enlightenment → self-elevation. Used as a tempering/modification of the pure derision account by inserting an epistemic sequence before the feeling of superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groos's inward imitation and aesthetic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second phase there is a moment of 'inward imitation' of the absurdity: the aesthetic attitude consists in transporting oneself into the object between deception and enlightenment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groos makes comic perception more 'aesthetic' by insisting that enjoyment is heightened when one previously participates in the absurdity one feels superior to; introduces the notion of 'fighting-play' as a playful, non-cruel derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ziegler / 'playful derision' (slight misfortunes)
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh at the stupidities and misfortunes of others only when they are slight and inconsequential; our scorn is essentially playful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualification of derision theory emphasizing the harmless, playful character of much laughter; explains why only slight misfortunes are comic rather than cruel Schadenfreude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schiitze's 'nature derides us' (object-as-derider)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative attribution: the mood of derision is ascribed to nature (the object) rather than the laugher — nature brings intended sublimities to a fall and thereby 'derides' us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the comic as a cosmic or external irony in which the world itself upsets our pretensions; offered as a contrasting way to locate the source of the comic (object vs subject).

rubrics_metrics.name: Schauer's teasing / joy of play
rubrics_metrics.description: All kinds of comic enterprise are identified with teasing: 'Teasing is a game in which the players take the role of adversaries... If the sport succeeds, it is... the joy of play.' He divides comic experience into objective-comic (we triumph) and subjective-comic (we are triumphed over).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recasts comic interaction as game-like rather than fundamentally egoistic hostility; suggests laughter stems from participation in playful roles and the enjoyment of being alternately hoodwinked or overcoming others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical challenge to universal superiority (Lillien J. Martin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental finding: when shown a comic picture, 37 of 60 reported a feeling of superiority but 23 (later 24 with the author) reported no such feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as evidence that the superiority/derision explanation does not account for all comic reactions; the author notes personal introspection about how being the object of laughter changes one's attribution (one would attribute scorn if oneself were laughed at).

rubrics_metrics.name: Association-of-ideas / quickness (Locke, Hutcheson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit lies 'most in the assemblage of ideas, and putting those together with quickness and variety' (Locke); Hutcheson adds laughter is caused by 'bringing together of images which have contrary additional ideas, as well as some resemblance in the principal idea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames humor as cognitive/syntactic skill: rapid association and juxtaposition of congruous and incongruous ideas (resemblance + contrast). Bain partly echoes superiority but these association accounts emphasize mental agility rather than hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bergson: laughter as corrective/humiliation of automatism
rubrics_metrics.description: In laughter 'we always find an unavowed intention to humiliate, and consequently to correct our neighbor...'; we laugh at the 'rigid, the ready-made, the mechanical' in contrast to the supple and living — laughter corrects individual or collective imperfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson insists laughter is incompatible with genuine emotion (sympathy/pity); the comic targets mechanical, automatic behavior in persons (or machines acting like persons and vice versa). The text critiques Bergson as treating the art of satire more than laughter per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voltaire: laughter from gaiety not contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Laughter always arises... from a gaiety of disposition, absolutely incompatible with contempt and indignation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posits a positive, genial character of laughter rather than a prideful or corrective one; cited to counter harsher versions of derision theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spinoza: moral distinction between derision and jest
rubrics_metrics.description: Derision is a form of hate and 'bad', whereas 'laughter and jest are a kind of joy, and so, if they are only not excessive are good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers an ethical appraisal: derision (mocking) undermines being, while playful jesting can promote well-being — distinguishes harmful mockery from benign laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kant's disappointment theory (strained expectation → nothing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is an affection arising from the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing; one must transform expectation into 'nothing' (not into an opposite) to produce laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the merchant story: build an expectation of anguish then end with 'nothing' to provoke laughter. The author notes Kant's insight is correct but inadequate — the 'nothing' can still have social/sentimental meaning producing 'sudden glory' (superiority) elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schopenhauer's incongruity/subsumption theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of laughter is the sudden perception of the incongruity between a concept and the real objects subsumed under it: all laughter is occasioned by a paradox or unexpected subsumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer reduces the ludicrous to a cognitive mismatch (concept vs particular); he further explains we enjoy the superiority of perception over abstract thought. The author critiques this as overly intellectual and not accounting for quick, reflexive, non-conceptual laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dumont's tickling/deceived-expectation experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh when expectation is deceived (e.g., pretending to pinch but not doing so); specific observations in tickling: (1) continuous unvaried touches do not tickle; (2) equal-interval touches do not tickle; (3) unexpected changes in interval or direction produce laughter; (4) varying rapidity or direction with unbroken contact can cause laughter; (5) one cannot laugh when tickling oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that laughter (in tickling) depends on variations and unexpectedness in temporal/spatial pattern rather than raw skin sensation, supporting a disappointment/deception component but with caveats that Dumont over-intellectualized the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play-attitude condition for laughter (Sully, Kiilpe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tickling (and other comic reactions) requires a particular mood: the 'play-attitude' or pleasurable condition of mind that welcomes fun; serious alarm, pain, or preoccupation blocks playful laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and observational support: children will not respond to tickling when frightened, ill, or preoccupied. Emphasizes that the nervous-system/play-state is a necessary condition for many forms of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/unexpectedness and the attenuation of jokes (Martin, Hollingsworth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects agreed that 'unexpectedness' and 'contrast' are always present in things they laugh at; jokes grow stale and lose comic quality as they become anticipated — Hollingsworth quantified rates at which jokes wane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for comedic production: novelty and unpredictability are key factors; familiarity reduces value, and different joke types wane at different rates (empirical curves).
